1.note: The author is speaking of a whole, **all of Israel**, to mean a part of that whole, representatives of the various Israelite tribes who **gathered to David**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And representatives of the various tribes of Israel]

The tribal representatives are using the term **Behold** to focus David’s attention on what they are about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

Here, **we are your bone and your flesh** was a common expression that the tribal representatives were using to affirm to David that they were related by descent from a common ancestor. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we are your blood relatives]

2.note: The tribal representatives are using **Both yesterday and the third day** as a common expression of his culture to mean the way things had been previously. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In the past]

The tribal representatives are speaking of a commander’s first and last actions in a military campaign, **bringing out** the soldiers to war and **bringing** them back **in** afterward, in order to mean military campaigns as a whole. Alternate translation: [the one leading Israel on military campaigns]

2.q: וַ⁠יֹּאמֶר֩ יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֶ֜י⁠ךָ לְ⁠ךָ֗ אַתָּ֨ה תִרְעֶ֤ה אֶת־עַמִּ⁠י֙ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְ⁠אַתָּה֙ תִּהְיֶ֣ה נָגִ֔יד עַ֖ל עַמִּ֥⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
2.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh your God told you that you would shepherd his people Israel and that you would become the ruler over his people Israel.]

2.q: אַתָּ֨ה תִרְעֶ֤ה אֶת־עַמִּ⁠י֙ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְ⁠אַתָּה֙ תִּהְיֶ֣ה נָגִ֔יד עַ֖ל עַמִּ֥⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
2.note: When Yahweh spoke to David as the representatives describe, he was stating the pronoun **you** separately in both of these instances, even though the verbs translated as **you will shepherd** and **you will become** already included this meaning, to emphasize that none other than David would do these things. If speakers of your language would use explicit pronouns for this purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [You are the one who will shepherd my people Israel, and you are the one who will become the ruler over my people Israel]

2.q: אַתָּ֨ה תִרְעֶ֤ה אֶת־עַמִּ⁠י֙ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְ⁠אַתָּה֙ תִּהְיֶ֣ה נָגִ֔יד עַ֖ל עַמִּ֥⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
2.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. It may be clearer in your language to connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [You are the one who will shepherd my people Israel; indeed, you are the one who will become the ruler over my people Israel]

Yahweh is speaking as if David would actually **shepherd** the people of Israel, as though they were sheep. This image compares the way a shepherd cares for and guides his sheep to the way a king should care for and lead his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You are the one who will care for and guide my people Israel]

3.note: The author is using **cut … a covenant** as a common expression of his culture to mean “make a covenant.” If this phrase would not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and David made a covenant with them]

Here, the **face** of Yahweh represents his “presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of Yahweh]

Here, **word** represents a message or prophecy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [according to the message from Yahweh]

Here, **hand** represents the agency of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that he had Samuel speak for him]

4.note: The author is saying **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [And David led a large army of Israelite soldiers]

The author is providing background information to explain to readers that the city they know as **Jerusalem** was known at the time as **Jebus**. In your translation, present this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The author is not referring to a specific **Jebusite**. He means the Jebusites who lived in this fortified area in Jerusalem. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the Jebusites]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **the dwellers of the land**, he means that the Jebusites were among the original inhabitants of the land of Canaan, before the Israelites arrived. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [some of the original inhabitants of Canaan]

5.note: The author is providing background information to explain to readers that the fortified area that he calls **Zion** is the same area that they know as **the City of David**. In your translation, present this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

6.note: See the discussion in the introduction to 1 Chronicles of how the author may use the term **striking** to mean “defeating” in battle. Alternate translation: [The first one to lead our soldiers to defeat the Jebusites]

The terms **head** and **chief** mean similar things. David was using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the leader of our army] or [my army commander]
The word **Zeruiah** is the name of a woman, David’s older sister.

See the discussion in the introduction to 1 Chronicles of how people in this culture generally indicated whether people were going up to a higher elevation or going down to a lower elevation when they traveled. (Since Jerusalem was on top of a mountain, Joab needed to go to a higher elevation to lead an attack against it.) If your language does not generally mark travel for change in elevation, you do not need to do that in your translation. Alternate translation: [went] or [led an attack]
See how you translated the term “head” in 5:7. Alternate translation: [and he became the leader]

8.note: The word **Millo** is the name of a place. (It was likely a raised platform or landfill that formed part of Jerusalem’s fortifications.)

9.q: וַ⁠יֵּ֥לֶךְ דָּוִ֖יד הָל֣וֹךְ וְ⁠גָד֑וֹל וַ⁠יהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת עִמּֽ⁠וֹ
9.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And since Yahweh of Armies was with him, David went, going and becoming great]

The author is using **went, going and becoming great** as a common expression of his culture to mean “kept becoming greater and greater.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And David kept becoming greater and greater]
See how you translated the similar expression in 9:20. Alternate translation: [Yahweh of Armies was helping him]

10.note: See how you translated the term “head” in 5:7. Alternate translation: [the leaders]

While this is a reflexive verbal form, the emphasis is not on what these **warriors** did for themselves but on what they did to help David. The idea is that they summoned their own strength on his behalf. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the ones who summoned their strength to help him]

The author is saying **all** as an generalization for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [with the other Israelites]

The author is using the term **word** to represent what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [according to what Yahweh had said]

11.note: See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of the differences in names between this list of David’s greatest warriors and the one in 2 Samuel 23:8–39. In 2 Samuel 23:8, this man may be called Josheb Basshebeth the Tahchemonite, or the text may mean “the Tahchemonite who sat in the chief seat.” Many scholars believe that 1 Chronicles presents the more ordinary forms of his personal and clan names.

The author is speaking as if Jashobeam’s **spear** had actually been asleep and he was **awakening** it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He aggressively used his spear as a weapon]

The author is using the adjective **Thirty** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase, here and throughout this chapter. It may be natural in some languages for the number to serve as a title or group name, as in the ULT. Alternate translation: [David’s 30 greatest warriors]

The phrase **the Thirty** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. There is, however, a correction in the margin of the text that Hebrew scribes have recommended. You may want to follow this correction in your translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [the officers]

The author is using the adjective **300** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing, a person, and specifically an enemy soldier. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [300 enemy soldiers]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. He is using simply the singular term **slain** to describe the state into which Jashobeam put these enemy soldiers. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [whom he slew]

12.q: וְ⁠אַחֲרָ֛י⁠ו אֶלְעָזָ֥ר בֶּן־דּוֹד֖וֹ הָ⁠אֲחוֹחִ֑י ה֖וּא בִּ⁠שְׁלוֹשָׁ֥ה הַ⁠גִּבֹּרִֽים
12.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that this man was **among the three warriors** before his name. Alternate translation: [And after him among the three warriors was Eleazar the son of Dodo, the son of Ahohi]

13.note: In this context, the term **people** means “soldiers.” Alternate translation: [the Israelite soldiers]

Here the phrase **from their face** is a common expression of the culture that means “from in front of.” The sense is that the Israelite soldiers knew that the Philistines were powerfully attacking them and so they no longer wanted to oppose them in battle. Alternate translation: [from the attack of the Philistines]

14.note: The pronoun **they** here and in the rest of the verse and the pronoun **themselves** refer to Eleazar and David. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But Eleazar and David stationed themselves]

The author is describing one event before describing another event that preceded it. If it would be helpful your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened. Alternate translation: [and they struck the Philistines, and they delivered it]
See how you translated the term “struck” in 1:46. Alternate translation: [and they defeated the Philistines]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh powerfully saved the Israelites]

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. The UST models one way to do that.

15.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 11:6. Alternate translation: [went]

The author is using the image of the **head** to mean a leader or chief. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the chief Thirty] or [the leading Thirty]
See how you translated the term “Thirty” in 11:11. Alternate translation: [David’s 30 greatest warriors]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **the rock**, he means the cliff in which the **cave of Adullam** was located. He assumes further that readers will know that David hid in that cave to escape from Saul, as 1 Samuel 22:1–22 describes. You could indicate these things explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to help David when he was hiding from Saul in the cave of Adullam, which was in a rocky cliff]

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.
The author is using the word **camp** to mean the Philistine soldiers who were in this camp. Alternate translation: [And a Philistine army]

16.q: וְ⁠דָוִ֖יד אָ֣ז בַּ⁠מְּצוּדָ֑ה וּ⁠נְצִ֣יב פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים אָ֖ז בְּ⁠בֵ֥ית לָֽחֶם
16.note: It might seem that saying “then” in both parts of this verse would be extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could say “then” in only one part of the verse, wherever it would be more natural in your language to say that.

17.note: Since what David says in the rest of the verse indicates what he **desired**, you do not need to explain that here at the beginning of the verse by saying something such as, “And David desired to have something to drink.”

17.q: מִ֚י יַשְׁקֵ֣⁠נִי מַ֔יִם מִ⁠בּ֥וֹר בֵּֽית־לֶ֖חֶם אֲשֶׁ֥ר בַּ⁠שָּֽׁעַר
17.note: David is using the question form to express his strong desire for water from the well. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I wish that someone would give me water from the well of Bethlehem that is at the gate!]

The term for **waters** is always plural in Hebrew. Different languages may need to use a singular form in certain contexts, as the ULT does in many other places and as the UST does here. However, since the Hebrew says **them** in the next verse, the ULT uses a plural form here. If your language would use a plural form in such a context, it would be appropriate to do that in your translation.

18.note: The author is using the adjective **three** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [And the three great warriors]

The pouring out of the water was a symbolic action by which David showed that this water, obtained at great risk by his men, was too precious to drink, and it deserved to be offered to Yahweh instead. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and he poured it out on the ground instead as an offering to Yahweh]

19.note: David is using a common expression of his culture to express his horror at the idea he describes. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [God forbid that I should do this!]

See the discussion in the introduction to 1 Chronicles of the Hebrew instructional form that the ULT represents with the English helping verb “shall.” Alternate translation: [Should I drink the blood of these men with their lives]

David is using the question form to emphasize that he should not do what he describes. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I should certainly not drink the blood of these men with their lives!]

David is using **with their lives** as a common expression of his culture to mean “who risked their lives.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the blood of these men who risked their lives]

David is speaking as if the water that the men brought were actually their **blood**. He means that the water represents the danger into which these men put their lives to get it for him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [this water that I am pouring out, since the blood of these men could just as easily have been poured out when they risked their lives to get it]
Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Alternate translation: [After all,]

The pronoun **them** refers to the “waters” the men got for David (v. 18). It may be more natural in some languages to use a singular pronoun. Alternate translation: [they brought it with their lives] or [they risked their lives to get it for me]

The author is offering a summary of the stories he has just related. This signals the end of this section about these **three warriors**. Use a natural way in your language to offer a summary that concludes a section. Alternate translation: [Those are some of the things that David’s three mighty warriors did for him] or [So ends the account of what these three warriors did]

20.note: The author seems to be describing two different groups of three warriors. In order to distinguish between them, the ULT treats the word **Three** as a title (uppercase) when it describes the great warriors of the first rank, Jashobeam (11:11), Eleazar (11:12), and an unnamed third warrior. It treats the word **three** as a description (lowercase) when it describes the great warriors of the second rank, Abishai (here and in the next verse), Benaiah (11:22–25), and another unnamed warrior. Your language may have a convention of its own that you could use to distinguish between these groups, or you could use descriptive phrases, as the UST does.

The author is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he was** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the identify of **Abishai** as the man who was the **head** of these warriors. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [he was the one who was the head of the three]

The author is using the image of the **head** to represent a leader or commander. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the commander of]
See how you translated the similar expression in 11:11. Alternate translation: [and he aggressively used his spear as a weapon]
See how you translated the same expression in 11:11. Alternate translation: [300 enemy soldiers, whom he slew]

Here, **name** represents reputation or honor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language, here and in verse 24. Alternate translation: [And he had as great a reputation as the Three]

21.note: The author is using the adjectives **three** and **second** as nouns. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjective with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [From the three warriors in the second rank, he was honored]

The author is using the term **From** to introduce a comparison. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [Of the three warriors in the second rank, he was the most honored]

The expression **was honored** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People honored him the most of the three warriors in the second rank] or [People honored him the most of the next three of David’s greatest warriors]

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **second**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use, or you could use an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [in rank two] or [next greatest warriors]

Here, **come to** represents joining or achieving the same level of status as the Three. The verse means that although Abishai was a great warrior and was highly honored, he did not achieve membership in or equal status with the Three. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, here and in verse 25. Alternate translation: [But he did not join the ranks of the Three] or [But he did achieve the same exploits and reputation as the Three]

22.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that Benaiah was **from Kabzeel** with the information that he was the **son of Jehoiada**. Alternate translation: [Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada, from Kabzeel, was a son of a man of valor, great of deeds]

In certain contexts, biblical authors and characters use the expression **son of** to indicate that a person has the characteristic of something. In this case, the author is saying that Benaiah has the characteristic of **valor**. Alternate translation: [was characterized by being a man of valor]

The author is using the possessive form to indicate that the **deeds** Benaiah did were **great**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [who did great deeds]

The author is stating the pronoun **he** separately in each of these instances, even though the verbs translated as **he struck** and **he went down** already include this meaning. He is doing that to confirm Benaiah’s exclusive personal role in accomplishing these feats. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for this same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that the author is confirming Benaiah’s exclusive personal role. It may not be necessary to represent the separately stated pronoun explicitly. Alternate translation: [He single-handedly struck … And he went down alone]
See how you translated the term “struck” in 4:43. Alternate translation: [he killed … and killed]

Interpreters do not understand exactly what the term **Ariel** means. However, many interpreters believe that it may be describing warrior champions as lion-like, that is, strong and fierce. Alternate translation: [two mighty champions of Moab] or [two fierce warrior heroes of Moab]

While the term **Ariel** is singular in the original, since the author is referring to **two** such people, it may be more natural in your language to use a plural form. Alternate translation: [Ariels]

23.note: See how you translated the similar expressions in 11:22. Alternate translation: [And he was the one who killed]

he author is using **a man of measure** as a common expression of his culture to mean a giant. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a giant]
The author is using the phrase **five by the cubit** to express height in a way characteristic of his culture. Alternate translation: [five cubits tall]

A **cubit** was an ancient unit of measurement corresponding to the distance between an average person’s elbow and middle fingertip, or about 46 centimeters or 18 inches. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this man’s height in modern measurements, either in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [seven and a half feet tall]

The point of this comparison is that just as a weaver’s **beam** is very thick and strong, so was the shaft of this man’s **spear**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [that was thick and strong, like a weaver’s beam]

The author seems to mean that Benaiah **went down** from the Israelite battle lines on a safe height, and he went into a valley to fight this **man of Egypt** in single combat between the battle lines. Alternate translation: [and he went into a valley to fight him in single combat]

24.note: The author is offering a summary of the stories he has just related. This signals the approaching end of this section about **Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada**. Use a natural way in your language to offer a summary that concludes a section. Alternate translation: [Those are some of the things that Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada, did as one of David’s warriors] or [So ends the account of Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada]

25.note: The author is repeating the term **him** for emphasis. It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [behold him, being honored]

The expression **behold him** is one that people of this culture would commonly use to mean that someone was about to do something, but in this context, the participle form **being honored** seems to indicate ongoing rather than imminent action. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he was continually honored]

The expression **being honored** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people continually honored him]

The author is speaking as if David had put Benaiah **over**, or physically above, his **bodyguard**. He means that David put Benaiah in charge of his bodyguard, that is, he made him the commander of those soldiers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And David made him the commander of his bodyguard]

26.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 7:5. Alternate translation: [And the very great warriors]

27.note: The names **Shammoth**, **Harorite**, and **Pelonite** are variant spellings of “Shammah,” “Harodite,” and “Paltite,” which are found in 2 Samuel 23:35–36. Many scholars believe that 2 Samuel preserves the more ordinary spellings of these names. The name “Elika the Harodite” appears between the names of these two men in 2 Samuel. See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of the differences between the names of warriors in this book and in 2 Samuel.

29.note: 2 Samuel 23:27 reads “Mebunnai” rather than **Sibbecai**. Most scholars consider Sibbecai to be the correct form of the name. 2 Samuel 23:28 reads “Zalmon” rather than **Ilai**. Most scholars consider Zalmon to be the more complete form of the name.
2 Samuel 23:29 reads “Heleb” rather than **Heled**. Most scholars consider Heled to be the correct form of the name.

32.note: 2 Samuel 23:30 reads “Hiddai” rather than **Hurai**. Most scholars consider Heled to be the correct form of the name. 2 Samuel 23:31 reads “Abi Albon” rather than **Abiel**. Abiel could be a shorter form of Abi Albon.

33.note: 2 Samuel 23:31 reads “Barhumite” rather than **Baharumite**. Most scholars consider Baharumite to be the more original form and Barhumite to be a variant spelling.

34.note: 2 Samuel 23:32 reads “the sons of Jashen” rather than **the sons of Hashem the Gizonite**. Scholars are uncertain which book preserves a more original reading. Some suggest that the texts should be read Beni Hashem and Beni Jashen and that both are developments of this man’s original name.

2 Samuel 23:32–33 reads “Jonathan; Shammah the Hararite” rather than **Jonathan, the son of Shagee, the Hararite**. Scholars suggest that the phrase “the son of” may have dropped out of 2 Samuel and that “Shammah” is more likely the original form, referring back to the man who is called “Shammoth” here in 11:27 but “Shammah” in 2 Samuel 23:35–36.

35.note: 2 Samuel 23:34 reads “Eliphelet, the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maacathite” rather than the way the text reads here. Eliphal seems to be a shortened form of Eliphelet. It is unclear whether Ur or Ahasbai is closer to the original form of this name. It is possible that the parallel in 2 Samuel should be read as describing two men: “Eliphelet, the son of Ahasbai; the son of the Maacathite.” The “son of the Maacathite” would then mean **Hepher the Mecherathite**, with Maacathite being the more ordinary spelling of the clan name.
2 Samuel 23:33 reads “Sharar” rather than **Sachar**. Most scholars consider Sachar to be the more original form.

36.note: 2 Samuel 23:34 reads “Eliam, the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite” rather than **Ahijah the Pelonite**. It is possible that Ahijah, “Yah is brother,” is a variant of Eliam, “God is kinsman,” and that the author is saying Pelonite, a reference to an indefinite person (“so-and-so”), so as not to name Ahithophel the Gilonite, the counselor of David who betrayed him. In that case, 2 Samuel would preserve the more original reading.

37.note: 2 Samuel 23:35 reads “Paarai the Arbite” rather than **Naarai, the son of Ezbai**. It is possible that Naarai and Paarai are variations of the same original name and that 1 Chronicles names this man’s father while 2 Samuel names his clan.

38.note: 2 Samuel 23:36 reads “Igal, the son of Nathan from Zobah; Bani the Gadite” rather than the way the text reads here. Scholars suggest that Joel is a simplified form of Igal, that Mibhar is an abbreviated form of “from Zobah,” and that Hagri is an abbreviated form of “the Gadite.” This suggests that the reading in 2 Samuel preserves the more original forms. It remains unclear whether Joel was the “son” or **brother** of **Nathan**.

41.note: From here to the end of the chapter, the author presents names that are not on the corresponding list in 2 Samuel 23:8–39. You should include all of these names in your translation, as these men were among David’s greatest warriors. The number Thirty (verse 11) is a round, symbolic number, and the Bible recognizes and honors a large number of warriors than that. (The parallel passage says “in all, 37” in 2 Samuel 23:39.)
